lesson.title: Writing the Rules: What a Rate Law Actually Tells You
lesson.summary: A rate law is an experimentally determined equation, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, that expresses exactly how a reaction's rate depends on reactant concentrations, and it must be measured in the lab, never assumed from the balanced chemical equation.
lesson.body:
Once you can measure an initial rate, the natural next question is: what determines its value? For most reactions, the answer is the concentrations of the reactants. A rate law is the mathematical expression that captures this relationship. For a reaction involving reactants A and B, the rate law takes the general form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where [A] and [B] are molar concentrations, k is a proportionality constant called the rate constant, and m and n are exponents called the reaction orders with respect to A and B.

This is the point in kinetics where a very common misconception needs to be confronted directly. It is tempting to look at a balanced chemical equation, say 2 NO + O2 leads to 2 NO2, and assume the exponents in the rate law must match the coefficients, giving rate = k[NO]^2[O2]^1. Sometimes that happens to be true, but it is not true in general, and you cannot assume it. The values of m and n are experimentally determined quantities. They have to be measured in the lab, typically using the method of initial rates covered in an upcoming chapter, and they reflect the actual step-by-step mechanism by which the reaction occurs at the molecular level, not the overall bookkeeping of atoms in versus atoms out that a balanced equation represents. A reaction can easily proceed through several elementary steps, and the slow, rate-limiting step among them might involve only some of the species, in proportions that have nothing to do with the final balanced coefficients.

Because reactant concentrations change throughout a reaction as products form and, in some cases, side reactions or reverse reactions become significant, rate laws are built from initial rate data. Chemists run a reaction several times, changing the initial concentrations of A and B in a controlled way from one trial to the next, and measure the initial rate each time. Comparing how the initial rate responds to each concentration change reveals the exponents m and n. That comparison process is the method of initial rates, and it is powerful enough to deserve its own chapter, but first it helps to understand precisely what k, m, and n mean on their own, which is where the next two chapters, on the rate constant and on reaction order, pick up.
